compliance.notes: Strongest area by a distance is the liability-benchmark work (LB-01/02/04 = 3): separate GF & HRA benchmarks built from the four balances, charted to ~2075 with a stated £10m liquidity buffer - Arlingclose-quality and a genuine sector model. Core prudential indicators, MRP policy, reporting cycle, governance and creditworthiness (INV-03 = 3, uses CDS/other data beyond ratings) are all solid, and a genuinely strategic Capital Strategy (CS-01 = 3) is in place. Weakest areas are the commercial/non-treasury and interest-rate-risk disclosures: proportionality of commercial investment (COM-03, core) is a single sentence with no quantified capacity test; there is no fixed/variable interest-rate exposure indicator (RISK-02, core); and several statutory commercial/investment disclosures are thin or missing (COM-02 paras 51-53, COM-09 investment limits, PI-08 income ratio, INV-05 specified/non-specified, BOR-03 sterling-only, RPT-05 audit-qualification flag). Context: distressed unitary under statutory intervention with Commissioners and a Capitalisation Direction; strategy is tightly focused on debt reduction and refinancing an under-borrowed (internal-borrowing ~£200m) position as legacy loans run off.

news_drafts.headline: Slough held 2025/26 overspend to £13.2m against £20.7m forecast, after £15.7m of support
news_drafts.lead:
Slough's external auditor reports that the council contained its 2025/26 overspend to £13.2m, against a forecast of £20.7m, after £15.7m of exceptional financial support (EFS), which is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The overspend was 7.5% of the £175.5m the council budgeted to spend. The auditor says the council "was successful" in containing it.

The auditor reports that spending controls introduced during 2025/26 reduced the forecast overspend, and notes that the measures did not address underlying demand growth. For 2026/27, the council was unable to set a balanced budget without £42.9m of additional EFS, approved in principle. Quarter one figures for 2026/27 forecast a £19m overspend for the year, which the auditor says may mean more EFS is required. When setting its medium-term plan, the council anticipated further EFS of £22.4m in 2027/28.

A separate report to the council, the interim auditor's annual report for 2025/26 and statutory recommendation, says that failing to address financial sustainability "risks the Council continuing to rely on exceptional financial support and borrowing to fund this". It states there are no direct financial implications from the interim report itself. Any additional investment and resourcing will be considered as part of 2027/28 budget setting.

news_drafts.headline: Slough forecasts £417.4m of exceptional financial support, £336.4m of it formally agreed to 2024/25
news_drafts.lead:
Slough Council's medium term financial strategy (MTFS) forecasts exceptional financial support totalling £417.4m, according to the draft budget update report for its Cabinet meeting on 16 November. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The paper says: "The agreed level of EFS as forecast in the MTFS totals £417.4m".

Of that total, £336.4m was formally agreed up to 2024/25. The remainder is set out year by year in the paper's table: £15.7m for 2025/26, £42.9m for 2026/27 and an indicative £22.4m for 2027/28.

The paper says the amounts for 2025/26, 2026/27 and the indicative 2027/28 are agreed in principle or indicative. It says they will be formally agreed only once the council's accounts have been audited and signed off.

news_drafts.headline: Slough's 2025/26 overspend came in at £13.2m against a forecast £20.7m; 2026/27 budget not yet balanced
news_drafts.lead:
Slough Borough Council ended 2025/26 with an overspend of £13.2m, after applying £15.7m of exceptional financial support (EFS), permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The council had forecast an overspend of £20.7m. Its external auditor's interim annual audit report says the forecast overspend "was contained" to £13.2m by year end.

The auditor attributes the reduction to measures introduced during the year, including freezing non-essential recruitment and reducing agency and interim staff. The overspend was predominantly in temporary accommodation and housing benefit subsidy loss, which together came to £13.8m.

For 2026/27, the auditor reports the council "has been unable to set a balanced budget" without additional EFS, with £42.9m approved in principle. The medium-term plan anticipated a further £22.4m in 2027/28. The council's Annual Governance Statement update for the second quarter rates red its inability to produce a draft budget for November that balances within its existing EFS assumptions. A detailed report on the budget and medium-term financial strategy is due at Cabinet in November 2026. The government's commissioners at the council describe financial sustainability as their "prime concern". The council's s.151 officer, its chief finance officer, said in a report to Full Council that it is not financially sustainable without EFS.

findings.headline: Council's actual interest rate performance was 4.06% in H1 2026/27, against average SONIA of 3.73%
findings.detail: The paper says the 4.06% compares favourably with average SONIA, and records Bank Rate at 3.75% for the period. Table 4 also shows a 4.06% weighted average rate on total investments.
findings.matters: A return above the benchmark rate on cash balances is a measure a finance director at another council can compare against their own treasury performance.
findings.figures: 4.06% actual rate; average SONIA 3.73%; Bank Rate 3.75%
findings.quote: The Council’s actual interest rate performance during the H1 2026/27 was 4.06% which compares favourably with the average SONIA rates as can be seen above.

findings.headline: PWLB HRA rate 0.4% below the certainty rate is available until March 2027
findings.detail: The paper says the discounted rate supports HRA borrowing and refinancing of existing HRA loans. There was no new HRA borrowing in H1 2026/27.
findings.matters: A discount with a fixed end date is a deadline for any HRA borrowing or refinancing, and the paper shows none was drawn in the first half of the year.
findings.figures: 0.4% below certainty rate; available up to March 2027
findings.quote: The PWLB HRA rate which is 0.4% below the certainty rate is available up to March 2027.

findings.headline: 10-year UK gilt yield rose from 4.86% at the start of H1 2026/27 to a high of 5.43%
findings.detail: The paper says the 20-year gilt yield moved from 5.45% to 5.93%, another high for the period. It links PWLB rates to gilt yields, and the paper attributes the rise to energy-driven inflation and a more hawkish outlook in the US and UK.
findings.matters: Gilt yields set the PWLB rates that councils pay on replacement funding, so a finance director at this council or a peer would weigh the timing of new borrowing against this movement.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt 4.86% at start, high of 5.43%; 20-year gilt 5.45% to 5.93%; SONIA averaged 3.73%
findings.quote: Over the period, the 10-year UK benchmark gilt yield started at 4.86% and ended at a high of 5.43%.

findings.headline: Treasury investments rose to £52.1m at 30 September 2026 from £19.3m at 31 March 2026, mainly on £24.5m of NHS grant
findings.detail: The paper says the increase in short-term investments is mainly driven by £24.5m of NHS grant receipts for the Upton Court development. It also reports £4.2m from asset disposals. Net borrowing fell by £42.9m in the half year to £407.6m at 30 September 2026. Average investment balances were £62.4m.
findings.matters: A large grant receipt held in short-term deposits shows how cash balances can move sharply within a half year, which affects the liquidity position a finance director has to manage.
findings.figures: Investments £19.3m (31.03.26) to £52.1m (30.09.26); £24.5m NHS grant; £4.2m asset disposals; average balance £62.4m; net borrowing £450.5m to £407.6m
findings.quote: Increase in short term Investments is mainly driven by receipts of £24.5m from NHS grant for Upton Court development

findings.headline: Expected DISH lease termination to add £2.5m to the General Fund and cashflow in 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper says Cabinet approved the lease termination for Development Initiative for Slough Housing Ltd in October 2026. It expects a positive impact of £2.5m on the General Fund and on cashflow in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A specific sum returned to the General Fund from a company arrangement is the kind of income change a finance director would track against the in-year budget, particularly alongside the SCF drawdown in the same paper.
findings.quote: there will be positive impact to the Council’s GF and its cashflow of £2.5m in 2026/27.

daily_post.headline: Council Tax collected 52.53% at Q2, 0.72% behind target; Business Rates collected 52.90%, 1.57% behind target
daily_post.lead: Collection rates behind target at mid-year show the cash timing risk a finance director would track against the full-year assumption, and a lender can compare Slough's collection against the Berkshire councils the paper refers to.
